own_scenes.desc: Lance Taylor, antiguo miembro de los Black Spades, reunió los elementos de la cultura (DJ, MC, graffiti y b-boying) en una sola comunidad, inspirado por la unidad del pueblo zulú: exmiembros de bandas convertidos en DJs, MCs, bailarines y grafiteros. Pinchaba en el centro comunitario de Bronx River y en el T-Connection de Ritchie T, rodeado de cajas de discos como «una caravana y la entrada de una banda». El «Maestro de los discos» lo mezclaba todo: rock duro, funk, clásica, go-go, música haitiana, salsa, la sintonía de Mi bella genio o «Mary, Mary» de los Monkees. De la Zulu Nation salieron los Jazzy Five y la Soulsonic Force; en los ochenta la Universal Zulu Nation llevó el hip hop por el mundo, de Japón a Sudáfrica, y le añadió un quinto elemento: el conocimiento.

notes.text: Bambaataa fue de los tres padres fundadores el que más influyó en el paso al vinilo. Con Arthur Baker y John Robie, en homenaje a Kraftwerk, grabó con la Soulsonic Force «Planet Rock» (1982): introdujo la caja de ritmos Roland TR-808 en el hip hop y lo fundió con la electrónica, «Numbers» más un ritmo de calipso. Sonó en el programa de Mr. Magic y Marley Marl en WHBI y dio vida al electro-funk; era, además, un disco espiritualmente consciente y futurista.

El Bronx que ardía: bandas, la tregua y el apagón de 1977

refs.q: It’s like a goddamn caravan, a combination of a caravan and a gang entry.
refs.para: I’m already thirty-two and the ferocity of the vibe, the electricity at the T-Connection, was turning me into a kid again. To see Bam and his DJs come to work. He had four guys behind him with record crates on their shoulders. It’s like a goddamn caravan, a combination of a caravan and a gang entry.

refs.q: So, if hip-hop is around the world as a music form, then seventy-five percent of it belongs to that Zulu Nation.
refs.para: Afrika Islam (DJ, Zulu Nation): Members of Zulu Nation are mastering their skill, being pulled out and planting seeds in all parts of the planet. As they flew out to Japan and China and Korea and California, they’re planting the seed because they were the real deal, how they act, walked, dressed. That’s some prophet shit, man. So, if hip-hop is around the world as a music form, then seventy-five percent of it belongs to that Zulu Nation.

Afrika Islam (DJ, producer): Bambaataa took it from Kraftwerk—Germans, who look like neo-Nazis, ain’t got no funky shit in their body at all, no soul at all—and adapted it in the Bronx, where it’s completely the opposite. And then, for it to be regurgitated, along with the funkiness of Bambaataa and the beats that were put down, which was more of soca, calypso beat, [the] drumbeat that’s put under it, and then the technology from [guitarist and synthesizer player] John Robie and Arthur Baker putting it together, then you had the minds that came together to put out something new. Technology meets creativity.

refs.q: “Planet Rock” is a hodgepodge between [Kraftwerk’s] “Numbers” and a calypso beat.
refs.para: “Planet Rock” is a hodgepodge between [Kraftwerk’s] “Numbers” and a calypso beat. And then with the greatness of the Soulsonic Force doing the rhyme style that they did, Mr. Biggs, Pow Wow, and G.L.O.B.E. putting it together, that’s what made it a complete thing.
